# Use feature-implement-loop

<!-- Generated by build_pack_guides.py from pack.json and the skills' own files. Edit those, not this. -->

Implement a feature or story so it ends up *verified*, not just generated. Takes a description + acceptance criteria, writes code and tests, then runs an adversarial review pass that hunts for gaps (broken edge cases, baked-in assumptions, uncovered acceptance criteria), and re-generates to close them — looping until the review is clean or a 3-round cap is hit.

**Reach for it when** handed a ticket / story / feature spec with acceptance criteria and the goal is shippable, self-checked code — not a first draft.

## Install it

```bash
npx skilldrop-cli install feature-implement-loop                 # Claude Code, your user folder
npx skilldrop-cli install feature-implement-loop --project       # Claude Code, this repo
npx skilldrop-cli install feature-implement-loop --ide cursor    # or kiro, codex, antigravity, copilot
```

It is part of the Dev team pack: [`--pack dev-team`](../packs/use-the-dev-team-pack.md) installs it with its neighbours.

## Ask for it

Say it the way you would to a colleague. Requests like these route to it:

- "Implement this ticket and make sure every acceptance criterion actually has a test"
- "Build this story, review your own code adversarially, and fix the gaps"
- "Here's a feature spec with acceptance criteria — give me shippable, self-checked code"
- "Implement the password-reset flow per these criteria and loop until the review is clean"

Requests like these belong to a different skill, so it shouldn't answer them:

- "Review this PR I wrote for edge cases and broken assumptions"
- "Should we use Postgres or DynamoDB for the new service? Write it up for review"
- "Run the pre-merge gate on my branch before I open the PR"

If another skill answers instead, ask for this one by name: "use feature-implement-loop".

## Check what you get

A good result:

- **Every acceptance criterion maps to a test by the final report.** A criterion with no asserting test is an ❌ open item — not a pass. This is the rule that makes the skill more than codegen.
- **The review challenges the code; it doesn't rubber-stamp it.** A round-1 review that finds nothing on a non-trivial feature is a smell — re-run it adversarially, assuming the first pass missed something (it usually did).
- **Tests assert behavior, not just execution.** ❌ a test that calls the function and checks it didn't throw. ✅ a test that asserts the criterion's expected output. Catch assertion theater in the review.
- **Regeneration is targeted.** Each round fixes the named gaps and leaves passing code alone. Don't rewrite the whole feature every round — that loses ground and never converges.
- **The cap is real.** 3 rounds, then stop and report. A loop that "just one more round"s past 3 is a bug. If it can't converge in 3, a human needs to see why.
- **The round log is honest.** If round 2 found nothing new, say so. If a gap was downgraded rather than fixed, say why. The log is the audit trail.

## Use something else when

- One-line fixes / trivial changes — the loop is overhead; just make the change.
- Greenfield spikes / throwaway prototypes — verifying code you'll delete wastes rounds.
- Specs with no acceptance criteria and none inferable — there's no gate to close. Get criteria first.
- Pure code *review* of code you didn't generate — that's [`devils-advocate`](../../../packs/dev-team/skills/devils-advocate/SKILL.md) standalone.
- Open-ended design questions ("should we use Postgres or Dynamo?") — that's `design-doc` + `doc-critique`.
